title: Data Manipulation: Transmitted Data Manipulation
summary: Transmitted Data Manipulation covers tampering with information while it moves between systems rather than after it is written to storage. The adversary places itself on the path, for example on a compromised network device, a malicious forward proxy, an injected library inside a data pipeline, or a middle position on an internal link, and rewrites fields inside the stream. Because the receiving side builds its stored record from the tampered stream, that record looks internally consistent, and integrity checks that compare the database only with itself will pass. Telemetry is usually indirect: Transport Layer Security (TLS) interception on hosts that should never terminate it, unexpected certificate authorities, new listening sockets on middleware, configuration changes to message brokers, and discrepancies between a sender's own application log and the receiver's stored values. Defenders separate this from legitimate activity by baselining which hosts may decrypt or rewrite traffic, which accounts may change broker configuration, and by reconciling source side and destination side records for the same transaction.

beginner.definition: Data manipulation means changing information so that it no longer matches reality. This version changes the data while it is travelling between two systems, not after it is stored. The data is correct when it leaves one place and wrong when it arrives at the next. The attacker sits in the middle of the path and edits the message on the way.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many business decisions rest on numbers that travel between systems, such as payments, stock levels and test results. If someone can change those numbers in transit, the organisation acts on false information. This kind of attack is quiet, because the saved record usually looks normal. It can cause wrong payments, wrong medical decisions or a hidden fraud that nobody notices for months. Detection is hard, so prevention and careful checking matter a great deal.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains a position on the network path, for example on a router, a proxy or a relay server.
They insert a tool that reads each message, changes chosen fields, and forwards the message onward without delay.
Because the change happens before storage, the receiving system saves the altered value as if it were the original.
The attacker may also edit logs or acknowledgements so that both sides believe the exchange was correct.
For payment or industrial systems they must learn the message format first, often over weeks of quiet observation.
If the traffic is encrypted, they break that protection with a rogue certificate or by controlling an endpoint.
beginner.example: Imagine a courier who carries order forms from a shop to a warehouse. A dishonest sorter opens each envelope, changes the quantity from ten boxes to one hundred, then seals it again. The warehouse trusts the paper, so it loads one hundred boxes and files the form. The shop's own copy still says ten. Nobody sees a break-in and no lock is forced. Weeks later the stock count is wrong, and the only clue is that the shop and the warehouse disagree.
takeaways: Data can be wrong even when every system looks healthy, so compare the sender's records with the receiver's.
Know which machines are allowed to read or rewrite traffic on the path, and alert when a new one appears.
Encryption only helps if the endpoints and the certificates along the path are genuinely trusted.

objectives: Explain what transmitted data manipulation changes and where in the path the change happens.
Identify the network and host log sources that could reveal tampering in transit.
Describe why a stored record can look correct even after the data was altered on the way.
Compare sender side and receiver side records to find a mismatch in a transaction.
Recognise legitimate decryption and proxy activity so that you do not raise false alarms.
